newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian dlr restrained in recent ranges.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian dlr restrained in recent ranges.

text.p: The Australian dollar spent its fifth straight session consolidating in a US$0.7835/7910 channel Monday and dealers expected the hiatus to linger a while yet.

The currency bowed beneath selling pressure for most of the day after its latest attempt at the upside ran into sizeable offers around US$0.7905 offshore. The strength of resistance encouraged a test of US$0.7860 support by range players, but this had so far proved equally stubborn.
Traders said market sentiment remained mildly bullish in the wake of the dollar's rally from US$0.7550 this time last month, but cautioned customers were in no hurry to chase it higher.

By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the dollar was pinned at US$0.7861/66 having bent to US$0.7862/67 at the start from Friday's late US$0.7893/89. Key levels were US$0.7835 and US$0.7910, and a break of either would likely release a 1/2 cent move.

The action was similar on the crosses where profit taking was evident after sizeable gains last week, but again support held firm with offshore investors remained content to be long of the dollar given its attractive interest diffrentials.
The currency was steady on the yen at 95.65/75 from 95.60/70 late Friday and softened a shade in trade weighted terms to 60.4 from 60.5, still not far from its December high of 60.6.
It also made noteable gains on sterling and the Canadian dollar, two currencies often regarded as competitors to the Australian dollar when it came to attracting offshore funds.

The dollar made it to 0.4901/07 stg from 0.4859/66 late Friday, its first trip atop 49 pence since early December, due in large part to an on-going re-appraisal of the monetary policy outlook here and in the U.K.

Yields in the latter had eased recently as speculation of a tightening in policy faded, while the curve here had shifted sharply higher as the market spun from discounting another cut in rates to contemplating a hike by year-end.
Some even harboured hopes the dollar's widening yield differential might lure back Japanese samurai bond investors once their financial year-end had passed on March 31.

Whether the market was justified in writing off another domestic easing might be easier to gauge after employment data for February were released on Thursday. A pickup in the pace of jobs growth in the second half of 1996 was cited by the Reserve Bank as one reason for its decision to put policy on hold.
Median forecasts are for a rise of 10,000 in employment following January's firm 28,400 gain, but estimates for this volatile series range from a 10,000 fall to an 18,000 rise.
A clue on what to expect should come from the ANZ job advertisements series for February out Tuesday, which have been a reliable leading indicator of job prospects in the past.
Ads rose 3.3 percent in January and another rise this time would be the first back on back gain since June.
The Westpac consumer sentiment index for March on Wednesday will provide an up-to-date indicator on consumer demand.

The index fell an unexpectedly sharp 7.9 percent in Febuary and analysts will be looking for a bounce this time, particularly as commercial banks slashed their mortgage rates in mid-February and most data in the last month has been upbeat.

Also out Thursday will be housing finance commitments for January, which analysts expect will show the impact of mortgage rate cuts delivered last year and rise around 4.0 percent on top of a 5.3 percent jump in December.
The longer term outlook for the dollar got a filip from strong February U.S. jobs data released Friday which pointed to continued fast growth in Q1.

Analysts felt the strength would gradually feed through to Japan and Europe, possibly delivering the sort of synchronised world pickup which would boost the demand for, and price of, commodities with benefits for the A$. -- Wayne Cole 9373 1800
